utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we are going to have the witness, I believe that the parties have something to raise at this stage. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. As you know, we are preparing for Mr. Butler to testify hopefully Monday, if all goes well. And in that regard, as he did in Krstic, the United States has requested that they be allowed to have a lawyer present in the courtroom during the initial questioning at direct examination and at cross-examination when issues of Mr. Butler's background may be at issue. As this Trial Chamber is aware, there are many people from the United States, from the UK, from France, and from other countries who have been allowed to work for and testify for this Tribunal on condition that they have a lawyer in the court, not to represent the individual but to represent the interests of the United States in this particular case, should any issues arise. Now, Mr. Butler was an active duty U.S. Army intelligence officer since 1991. He was seconded to this Tribunal in April 1997 and he retired from the U.S. Army in September 2001 and has been working as a UN person here. Since then, though, he left in September 2003. And he again expects to work for the United States government in January. The United States has asked me to merely request to the Court your permission to have a United States lawyer here for those times when he is questioned about his background and of course any other time that an issue may arise, though if it happens, what happened in Krstic they were just here for the first 30, 40 minutes, and then once we got into the relevant, substantive matters, there was no need to. So that is my first request for the United States. I, of course, do not represent the United States, but just out of a matter convenience and time saving, we thought this would be a good way to do it. I have spoken to counsel a few times over the last several weeks about the areas of Mr. Butler's testimony, and of course it's wide open on any work that he did for the UN. And I know that Mr. Karnavas has studied what happened in the Krstic trial and appears -- doesn't have any problem with working within the limits that were described. Fundamentally, Mr. Butler's background is also open. His education that he did as a military officer and his resume will be introduced that shows the various assignments that he had over the years which include places like Somalia and Iraq. What he can't answer questions about are the specifics of what he was doing in those various jobs or the United States capabilities regarding intelligence gathering, be that aerial imagery or intercepts. And he, of course, will not be testifying about anything regarding U.S. aerial imagery or intercepts. That -- the aerial imagery has come in through Mr. Ruez, as you're aware, and he'll talk about Bosnian intercepts. U.S. Intercepts, I'm not aware of any or their capabilities at this point. But it's really, of course, not relevant. I don't think that's a problem in terms of speaking with the Blagojevic team. In speaking to Ms. Sinatra, she may have some concerns in that area and may need to be -- I'm sure she will want to be heard on that. So my first request is: May the United States have a lawyer here during these brief times and also, if we cannot reach an informal agreement as to the questioning of Mr. Butler, I will be presenting, I imagine, if the Court so deems, a written -- asking for an order for the various parties so that it's clear from the Court's order what they can question on and what they can't. I'm hoping that wasn't necessary, but maybe it might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any comments on submissions? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I did speak with Mr. McCloskey regarding this. He did bring it to my attention a few weeks ago. I also went through transcript where a similar request was made. I'm familiar with Mr. Butler's work product. As fascinating as the area that we cannot get into might be, on a personal level I understand it's not relevant to this case and therefore I do not intend to even attempt to go into those areas and I respect the U.S. government's concerns regarding that. As far as having a lawyer present, I really have no objections to that. Even if the lawyer wishes at some point to address the Court, if they deem it necessary to advise us that we're getting into areas which might be sensitive. So I think it's a reasonable request on behalf of the Prosecutor. It was brought to my attention early on for me to react and respond and think about it so I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This issue was brought to my attention and Mr. Stojanovic's attention yesterday for the first time that there was the possibility that the U.S. government was requesting an attorney to sit in the courtroom. The way Mr. McCloskey has stated it is that he will be plain clothed. I believe he's a member of the CIA. He is a lawyer, supposedly. And if he's a lawyer, Your Honour, we certainly think that it is outside of the normal procedures of this Trial Chamber, because all the Dutch military experts have come to testify. We've had military experts from all other countries, and I don't believe that they required a protection in the courtroom other than our UN security officers. And if they feel threatened, then they have a right to sit here in the anti-courtroom like everybody else does. If they want to appear in this courtroom as an attorney, then they should ask the Court's recognition, they should robe up and they should be specific about what their intentions are here in the courtroom. But just to have someone in plain clothes coming in and out of this courtroom, maybe even sitting through private sessions and confidential information offends these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This has been a tradition in this Tribunal for as long as its been in existence. Most recently there was a UK lawyer sitting in for the testimony of Ewan Brown in the Brdjanin and Talic case. There is no mystery. There's no espionage. This is the daily business of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra, I think we fully understand your concern unless you have something more to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I forgot that his presentation today is two-fold. It's not just the presence of somebody else in the courtroom, another counsel for another country. But also he described limiting the scope of cross-examination of Richard Butler. If Mr. McCloskey would like to stick to the facts of Krstic case and not present the new evidence regarding the Zvornik Brigade and regarding intercept evidence, then we would not pursue this area. But we have a right to test this expert's knowledge. We can ask him if he knows. If he doesn't know, then we won't go into it. This is a very major issue in the Defence of Mr. Jokic. They're presenting their military expert here. We have a right to test his knowledge on the capabilities of the United States government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber heard the oral application for the presence of the representative of the U.S. government during Mr. Butler's testimony. We regarded it as a kind of protective measure sought by the Prosecution under Rule 70 and 75 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal. The Rule 70 stipulates matters not subject to disclosure, which specifically mentioned the matter of confidentiality. There were several matters concerning the confidentiality this Trial Chamber should be carefully regarded. For instance, the privileges of the communication between the counsel and his client. The doctor/patient relationship, as well as the state interest and the secrecy. In the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, there are many precedents in this respect. In the Tuta and Stela case, a motion was filed requesting the presence of a representative of a humanitarian organisation during a witness's testimony. The reason of the motion is if it is widely and publicly known that his staff is testifying before the ICTY, his staff currently in the former Yugoslavia and else where may be subject to revenge attacks or intimidation. That Trial Chamber granted a motion and allowed counsel of the humanitarian organisation to be present in the courtroom to assist the witness and the Trial Chamber on questions of confidentiality that might arise in the course of the testimony. In the Galic case, the Prosecution requests the presence of a representative of a French government in the courtroom during their testimony. The Trial Chamber granted a motion saying that it can reasonably allege that the testimony of the witness might endanger the safety of the French civilian and military personnel currently deployed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and thereby infringing upon the national, diplomatic and military interests of France. In the Stakic case in which Judge Vassylenko and Judge Argibay were sitting on that Bench, two representatives of the UK were present while a military expert from the UK was testifying. They were authorised to make submissions whether or not fundamental interests of that country could be infringed by what has been said or is said in this courtroom. It is well known that the same practice was followed in the Krstic case, which is closely related to this case. Therefore, in this case the Trial Chamber decided to grant the oral motion by the Prosecution, allowing the representative of the U.S. government to be present during the testimony of Mr. Butler to make submissions on whether or not the fundamental interests of the U.S. government could be infringed upon. At the same time, the Trial Chamber believes that by granting this kind of protective measures, it would not infringe upon the rights of the accused to a fair trial. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I leave to get back to work on other matters before the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope you could stay a little bit longer. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm really sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Of course, I totally respect the decision of the Trial Chamber in that area, but also Mr. McCloskey was limiting the scope of cross-examination, basically telling us that we cannot go into areas that are relevant and germane to the Defence of Mr. Jokic. So I would like the Trial Chamber to consider this and tell us whether we can go into areas that we need like to explore. If he's got all this protection, if he's got his counsel in the courtroom, then there's use of private session, there's use of closed session, but for the record we need to explore these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what kind of areas you are going to explore. I believe that this Trial Chamber would make decisions on the case-by-case issue, especially during your cross-examination. Thank you. And another matter is that the other day Mr. Karnavas proposed two documents to be tendered into the evidence, that is the document D73 and D74, if I remember rightly. And Ms. Issa has promised to convey this idea to Mr. McCloskey, the lead counsel, whether the Prosecution agreed or not. Could I hear from the Prosecution on those two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think D72/1 is a newspaper article which we had no objection for. And the other document was a witness statement for a witness that has testified and we would object to that along the grounds that we have normally gone under, plus we didn't have an English version of that until after he testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, as for the statement of the witness is on the different occasions is not a statement before our Tribunal. It's a statement before other judicial organs, if I remember rightly, which makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If Your Honours feel this will be something that will assist them, I have no objection. I believe it was a statement to the police department -- a statement given to the police in Republika Srpska. But I have no objection. If you feel it's going to provide you some value, we would not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly. For the record, Your Honour, it's my understanding that we're speaking about D71/1, and that would be the interview that the gentleman had given to the Bratunac police station back on 25 August, 2003. And then D72 is the article that appeared in the newspaper. It just briefly -- Mr. McCloskey wasn't here to hear my argument regarding these two documents, but the article itself is what triggered then the investigation by the local police. And the gentleman does make references to the article, in that he disagrees with contents of the article which appear to have been direct quotes from the statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility of Mr. Nikolic. Also, the gentleman did indicate that after reading the article and after being interviewed by the police, he was waiting for OTP to perhaps contact him, as they had in the past, to provide further clarification or take a second statement. So I do think that they are relevant and particularly the statement itself I think dovetails his testimony, lest there be any misunderstandings that the gentleman perhaps was fabricating what he was saying here or was being less than honest or less than complete. I think it all demonstrates that he went before an independent body that did an investigation that was triggered as a result of the Nikolic's statement of facts being published. That the statements that he gave to the police are consistent with the statement that he had given to the Prosecutor, albeit not the same, because the same questions were not being asked. And that it was consistent with the statement that he had given here. And it also ties in with the other witness's statement that testified at the Nikolic sentencing hearing in that the denial of one particular aspect of Mr. Nikolic's testimony dealing with the six killings. So I think it's highly relevant. It's highly probative. And I think the Court should give it considerable weight, although I leave that to the Trial Bench. But I do think that this is appropriate and it is not the same sort of statement that the Court has ruled on in the past, where the OTP has taken a statement, then the witness comes in and testifies. And I'm in agreement in those instances, the whole statement shouldn't come in, perhaps portions of it. Here we're talking about a quite separate situation. And therefore, perhaps now that Mr. McCloskey has heard the argument, I am sure he can reflect and perhaps join me in agreeing that the documents should be admitted for the Court's consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas, for correcting me on the numbers of those two documents. Since there is no objections on the part of the Prosecution, so the document D71/1 and D72/1 are admitted into the evidence. It is so decided. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. You may withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be back on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Davis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we begin, I want to assure you that, as you probably can tell, there are protective measures in place, that your image is being distorted for the purposes of the outside world and that you're testifying under a pseudonym. And I would ask you if at any time during my questioning or subsequent questioning by the Defence or by the Trial Chamber, if you're asked a question to which you can't respond without providing identifying information, if you would let me know or let the questioner know and then we can go into a private session. If I could have the usher's assistance to provide the witness with what's been marked for identification as P351. Witness, if you could just take a look at that and verify that your name is written on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I completed secondary school, eight years of education, and secondary school which entailed three years of education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during your secondary school years, did you have any experience or training with radio communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: During my education, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about outside of formal education, did you have any training during those years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I was a member of a radio amateur club where I lived. In 1984 I obtained the C grade certificate for radio amateurs. It was a hobby for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's involved in obtaining a C grade classification -- certificate, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: -- I got was a driving license. This is a radio amateur license, grade C or category C --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But according to the witness list of the Prosecution that we were preparing with, this is not the witness that was listed next to appear on their list. We may need a few moments to get our files organised because we were expecting another witness, another protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is there any change of the order of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour, but we can double check on the list we provided to the Court and to the Defence. I believe this was the next witness listed, but we can double check if you give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: With permission and the assistance of the usher, I would provide our list of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe this is an outdated list. I think we have updated it since then. I'm not sure. Maybe Mr. Karnavas could be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go into closed session -- private session, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, wait. Yes, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Are we now in open session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what's involved in obtaining a C category certificate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: In order to obtain a C category certificate, you needed to be able to receive a certain number of Morse code signs per minute and you needed to be able to type them at the same speed. You needed to be familiar with international codes for countries, especially when surrounded. And you needed to know international abbreviations for establishing communication. You also needed to be familiar with antennas and with the equipment that you were expected to work with. I'm referring here to the radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you learn what you've just described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I learned this from my friends in the town where I was born. After I completed my training, there was an exam we had to take before a committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time later on when you obtained an additional certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I obtained a B category certificate. That was in 1993, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at some point serve in a mandatory -- provide mandatory service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the JNA, in Pristina, that is in Kosovo, from

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of equipment did you use or did you receive any training in any particular radio communications equipment during your service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: There was Russian equipment in the armoured vehicles. Those were large devices and we were not trained to use those as standard equipment in our first six months of training. We were self-taught, we used handbooks to learn that. We used manuals to learn how to operate those Russian devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from the Russian devices, were there other radio communications equipment that you learned to use during the course of your service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: During the course of service in the JNA, everyone learned how to operate the various RUPs. Those were hand-held devices, RUP-12 or PRC, which was produced in Canada, and we had another device that was produced in Yugoslavia also called PRC. Those were radio sets. In the other half of our training after our initial training, the other six months, we were taught how to use the radio relay device number 1, and we had some superficial training in operating the HVT radio relay. We were taught about its spare parts, components, and so on, nothing very specific, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that you were trained in how to use radio relay device number 1. Is there a specific name for that device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The abbreviation is RRU-1, which means radio relay device number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the HVT radio relay, is there another name for that device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: HVT, no, there is no other name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the -- your compulsory service in the JNA, I believe you said it was in December 1989, and were once again a civilian, did you have an opportunity to put your radio communications experience to use?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I was still a member of the radio amateur club, and we took part in competitions that were organised every first weekend of the month. Those were radio amateur competitions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your training in the use of radio communications equipment continue after you left the compulsory service in the JNA, whether formal or informal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Well, yes, I took part in those competitions, which was some form of training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I joined the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to which unit did you belong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I joined the electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention specifically to July 1995, can you tell the Trial Chamber where you were stationed at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: In July 1995, I was stationed at Konjuh. It was a separate feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you -- were you at Konjuh with the electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic warfare unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was. I was still in the same unit at that time. We carried out reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could explain in a little more detail what your duties and responsibilities were. I'm going to ask you momentarily to take us step by step through some procedures, but if you can just describe generally what your duties and responsibilities were at Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I have to remind you that the word the counsel has spoken to you at the beginning of the direct examination. You have to be very careful. Do you know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go into private session momentarily, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You may proceed, Ms. Davis. Shall we go to private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Yes, if we could just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were describing for us, witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were describing for us, Witness, generally what some of your duties were while you were stationed at Konjuh. What was the responsibility of the unit as a whole at Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The unit at Konjuh monitored the Drina Corps zone and the general staff, that's their communications, their communication lines, the lines of the Drina. That is, we covered a zone between Zvornik, that's to the left, to the east, and then to the south all the way to Sarajevo. That was our zone. That's what we monitored from Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do I understand that you were monitoring communications of the VRS within the region that you described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We were monitoring communications within that zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the Drina Corps and the Main Staff. Were there other units or subordinate brigades of the VRS that you were monitoring in July 1995 at Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: When I referred to the Drina Corps, I meant the communications of the subordinated brigades at corps level. I also meant the links between the corps and the general staff, well some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher. This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I'm showing the witness Exhibit P318.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could use the pointer and indicate on the map the location of Konjuh where your unit was positioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Konjuh is right here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We can leave that on the ELMO for the moment. Can you describe the location, can you describe Konjuh where your unit was positioned from a geographical perspective.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Well, Konjuh is an elevation of 1.326 metres high. The reason the unit was stationed there was in order to be able to better monitor the radio relay communications. This is a dominant feature in this particular area of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were in Konjuh as of July 1985. Can you tell us when you arrived at Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: 1985, that was the interpretation I got. It wasn't in 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for the confusion. What I meant to ask was before you left Okresanica and went to Konjuh, had you ever spent any time at this location in Konjuh before prior to May 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. Back in 1984 when I obtained my radio amateur certificate. There were competitions, radio amateur competitions, as I said ever first weekend of the month. And we would go to Konjuh sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why would the amateur -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I mean, we didn't enter the military facilities there, because those were occupied by the JNA. In addition to our antenna we also had a small shack that we built for ourselves and a tent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did the amateur ham radio club go to Konjuh for competitions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: We used to go there because that is an elevation. It's a very dominant position. The so-called DX communication was possible and the range is over 3.000 kilometres. You had to take into account the distance involved. The more communications you had, the better the range was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned also a moment ago that you had been at Okresanica. Can you tell us when you were at Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Okresanica, I can't remember the exact date. First we were in Lipik which was near Okresanica. Lipik is smaller than Okresanica itself, and then we crossed over to Okresanica itself, because that was a more dominant feature in the area, which made our monitoring activity easier. But I can't remember the exact date. It was perhaps about -- well, I don't know, but I do remember that it was wintertime back in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were at Okresanica you believe from winter 1993 and were you up there until May of 1994 when you went to Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you also indicate the location of Okresanica on the map that's on the ELMO to your right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Okresanica is further north from Konjuh or Tuzla, if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on Konjuh and the period July 1995. Can you tell me how many soldiers were working in that unit intercepting communications in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: There were two shifts usually at the location. One shift were us and the second shift was there close to a location. There were about ten of us. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you meant when you said there were two shifts and the second shift was there closed to a location. Could you explain that again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: One shift was from one town and the other was practically, let's say, from a different town. So from my town, there were about ten of us. And this other team would be at home at that time. We had shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us again how long the shifts were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: It depended on the fuel. From seven to ten days, sometimes it would be up to 14 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after a seven- to ten-day shift, your group would be replaced by the second group. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. Then we would go home to rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the seven- to ten-day shifts, what was your work schedule?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: We worked in the workroom where the equipment was. The shifts were of four hours length. We would work for four hours, and then we would rest for eight hours. And then we would come back to the shift again, except the night shifts. The night shifts were longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were the night shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think they were eight hours long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the room where the equipment was. Can you describe the equipment that you all used to intercept communications at Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This was amateur equipment that you could practically buy in town, here specifically. The receivers were also there. We actually had the transceivers, but we received them at receivers -- we used them as receivers. We also had amateur receivers that we were using. This wasn't professional equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the transceivers that you used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: They were short wave transceivers, and so they could only be used for receiving as well as transceiving. We were using them for reception but they also had the possibility to search channels by frequency. The equipment that we used was generally equipment of Japanese manufacture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the brand names of the transceivers that you used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: It was Kenwood, Icom, AR receiver also. So these were mostly the devices that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall specifically in July 1995 what type of transceivers were being used at Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: These devices were also used at Okresanica. The Kenwood 450S, Icom 100 or ICR100, Icom ICR7000, ECR7000, R -- ECR71 [as interpreted], which was also an Icom piece of equipment. So this was mostly the equipment that we used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from transceivers and receivers, did you also have tape recorders at Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Besides that equipment, we also had UHER tape recorders of German manufacture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many work stations, if you can remember, were there, approximately, at Konjuh? How many individual operators could be working at once monitoring frequencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The Konjuh facility had three stations to monitor multi-channel radio relay communications. We also had two, three, or more RRU-1s to monitor single channel radio relay communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a photograph that has been marked for identification as P319. And I would ask you if you recognise this piece of equipment. I don't know if it's going to appear on your monitor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is it, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: On the left side of the picture is a Kenwood TS450S, in this case 450S. This is a transceiver. And then on the right side, we have an Icom ICR100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what did the piece of equipment on the left, what its function is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: In this combination with the ICR100 device, this piece of equipment was used to separate channels. So we had 24 memorised channels programmed into it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could have you look now at what's been marked as P320 and ask you as well whether you recognise this piece of equipment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This is an UHER tape recorder report 4000, I think, R4000, that was the model.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these UHER tape recorders used in combination with the equipment you saw in the other photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: They were used to record from this device, from the Kenwood device.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could describe for the Trial Chamber the procedure that you used using the equipment that we've seen in these photographs to monitor conversations, starting from the beginning of the process, if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: When we came into the workroom, somebody would always be there. Somebody was also there through the night. So if you worked the first shift, somebody would already be there. I would usually be the first person to come. I would ask if there had been any traffic. Was there anything in particular. Then that person would convey that to me. Then I would take his place. The equipment was already scanning usually, that's what we would call it, scanning, searching. So it would be skipping from one memorised channel to the next. When a conversation occurred, then I would stop the scanning, I would find the channel where the conversation was taking place, and I would begin to record on the tape recorder, and I would also listen to that conversation, unless I had another piece of equipment next to me. Because we would also combine this with the monitoring of single-channel frequencies. For example, we would be monitoring the RRU-1. I was now talking about the monitoring of multi-channel traffic, which would be done by the RRU-800 equipment. I would tape the conversation. Afterwards, I would stop the tape recorder. When I taped the conversation, I would write down the frequency and the channel on the piece of paper where this was recorded on the UHER or the tape recorder, if there was a counter. So if the counter was working, I would write down the number. I would note down the number where it began and then when the conversation was finished, I would note down the number on the counter as well. If I had listened to the conversation, I would note down something which would remind me or associate me with that conversation. So this is what I would use a piece of paper for. After the conversation was complete, I would again initiate the scan function. If another conversation occurred, I would record that. I would stop the scanning. I would initiate the recording function. I would note it down. So I would use the same procedure. If I was listening, then I would note down a few remarks about the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. You mentioned that when you found a conversation, when the scanning landed upon a conversation you would begin to tape record, did you always begin the tape recording at the beginning of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Since the device would be scanning, sometimes it would not catch the beginning of a conversation. But in any case, it would always stop and I would continue the taping regardless of whether it was the beginning or the middle of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that you noted down on a piece of paper some details about the conversation. Can you tell us precisely what information you would note down on a piece of paper when you stopped the machine and began -- stopped the scanning and began tape recording.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: A piece of paper, I would write down -- on the piece of paper I would write down the frequency, the channel, the counter number, and I would also jot down names if I heard any names or I would jot down something from the conversation or what they were talking about. For example, if they were looking for tyres, I would say something about tyres, so that I would know what the conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And before that, Ms. Davis, can I ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If I just might assist. This is a different location and we're quite curious as to what evidence they have at this location versus the other one that the witnesses have testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I certainly would not be raising any objections. You know, in other words, I would be willing to stipulate.

utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Yes, I was just confirming that the witnesses thus far had all been from Okresanica and that was the reason I was going through the same steps. But I can certainly try and streamline it. I don't expect to have more than another half an hour with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we'll resume at 4.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break you were telling us that you -- at the time you began tape recording a conversation you would note down an a piece of paper some particulars. One of the things you mentioned was participants. I would like to ask you how did you identify participants to note them down on a piece of paper? What were the various ways?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: There were cases when the participants themselves introduced themselves during the conversation, at the beginning of the conversation. When we wouldn't catch the beginning of a conversation, then we knew many of the participants in the telephone conversations by their voices. So we would write down the name based on that. Then by listening later, we would determine whether that was that participant or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you finished tape recording a conversation, what would you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: After recording the conversation, we would then allow the scanning function to continue until we would tape a certain number of conversations. And then after a certain amount of time, I would begin to transcribe the conversations down on paper. I would let the device continue scanning, and I would continue taping if there were more conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say you would transcribe the conversations down on paper, where would you transcribe them in particular? Was it into notebooks or the scraps of paper we were talking about earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: When I began transcribing the conversation, I would wind back to the first conversation, if there was several conversations. I had a notebook at that time. Before we were transcribing the conversations on pieces of paper in earlier years, but at that time we already had notebooks where we would note down the frequency, the time, and the channel. So we would put that down in the notebook. Then we would write down the participants, if we knew them, the names of the participants, their rank if we knew it. And then we would take down the conversation itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the process for taking down the conversation from the tape, if you could just tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The process was as following: After recording, I would play back a small portion of the conversation, write it down, pause, write it down, and then I would continue until I completed transcribing the entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you do if there was a portion of the tape that you couldn't understand the first time through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: If I couldn't understand a part of the recording, I would call a colleague or several colleagues. So several of us would check, because perhaps some one might hear it a little better. If we were not sure about a certain part of the tape, we would put down dots. But if we were sure, then we would transcribe what was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you described to us some various ways which you might identify participants, what would you do if you didn't -- weren't able to identify a participant, either by voice recognition or self-identification? What would you write down in the notebook if you didn't know the participants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: If we didn't know the participants, then we would write down participant X or participant Y or we would mark them by numbers, 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you had finished transcribing the conversation in the manner in which you described, what would you do with the notebook or what would you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The notebook would be given to the person who would be typing the reports into the computer. So it would be given to this person for him to transfer the text on to the computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to the information that was transcribed into the computer after that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: There was a person there who when we compiled enough conversations that were transcribed into the computer, we would send a telegram. We would encrypt it and then send it on to the command through our communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the information once it was sent to the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The information was processed down there. There was a team responsible for analysis of data and they would process that and pass that on to their superiors, all the intelligence data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you responsible for performing any analysis of the data that you were -- the conversations that you were monitoring and transcribing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: No, we were not responsible for the processing of the data. We were responsible for transcribing the conversations from the tapes to the paper, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you what has been marked for identification as P335. And if I can ask you, sir, to turn to the page in the notebook that is marked with the number at the top of the page 0080 -- perhaps the usher can help you -- 0871.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I see the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, do you see a date on the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the date that's written there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: It is the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that written in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me from looking at this what the notebook that you're holding in your hands is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This is the notebook from my unit while I was at Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if this is -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This is an intercepted transcribed conversation which I had transferred from the UHER to the notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the first conversation that appears on that page 0871, can you tell us what time were whether a time is reflected for that intercept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, you can see the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the time that is reflected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: It's 9.00 and 5 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you transcribed from the UHER into the notebook, how would you have known the time to write down there in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: When the conversation was taped from the device to the UHER tape recorder, I would write down the time, the frequency, and the channel on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the scrap of paper that you were describing before, in addition to the frequency and the channel, you would also write the time the conversation started. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what can you tell for this particular intercept about the channel and the frequency on which it was found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This is 872.500 frequency. It was recorded on channel 9 at 5 past 9.00 from a multi-channel transceiver -- from a multi-channel radio relay device RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance for one moment. I'm giving to the witness now what's been marked as P226. And, Madam Usher, if you could have the second page which is 226/B showing on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Witness, this isn't the best copy, but I wonder if you could confirm for me that P226/B, which is showing on the ELMO, is a photocopy of the page that we were discussing in the notebook, 0871.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, this is a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what's written beneath the -- on the next line after the channel and the frequency information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The participants in the conversation, the duty officer, and General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that it says the duty officer. I notice that that's not a specific name. Does that mean that you didn't recognise the voice of this participant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't recognise the duty officer's voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you determined that it was the duty officer speaking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The General repeated after him, the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next participant listed is General Zivanovic. Can you tell us how you would have recognised that it was General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Well, he often took part in these conversations, and we were familiar with his voice, most of the operators were. He had a very peculiar kind of phone that he was using. I'm not sure if it's his voice or the phone that was the basis of this particular identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times would you estimate that you heard General Zivanovic speaking over intercepted communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what the number was, but from 1992 and 1993 we would monitor him regularly because he spoke regularly. I can't give you the exact number of times that we did, but he spoke very often because he was the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you estimate that you heard his voice hundreds of times --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thousands of times --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. She can ask the question how often he heard. But to be giving the witness suggestions as to how many times is clearly inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Davis, you have to lead us step by step.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you give us any estimation of how many times you heard General Zivanovic speaking over the radio between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Well, he would speak regularly every morning. He would talk to his subordinates every morning, so to speak. Now, as for the exact number, I spent a lot of time in the field, but I listened to him very often. In addition to his regular appearances, he would run his daily business over the phone, but I can't give you the exact number. But in those years, those two years or whatever, he was being monitored.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If the usher could turn to I believe it should be /C of the same exhibit. Sorry. The original version, not the translation. Maybe it's /D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA

utterances.text: Well, Ms. Davis.

utterances.text: I see. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, looking at the page that's now appearing on the ELMO which should be /D of this exhibit, 226, can you tell me whether you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I recognise this. This is a typed up copy of the conversation that I did on the computer. This was printed from a computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the format as something that's familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with this header. That's what we usually wrote or typed into our computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this the type of document you were referring to earlier when you mentioned that the transcribed conversations in the notebook were typed into the computer and sent to the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the second conversation that appears on the page, I notice that there is something that says "zone 2," at the beginning of the conversation. Can you tell me what "zone 2" means.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Zone 2 is the zone that we monitored. It's the zone stretching south from Zvornik towards Sarajevo. That's the name we used for that zone, zone 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would, Witness, turn the page in the notebook that you have before you, which again is for the Court's reference Exhibit P335. If you could turn the page to 0872, there is a second conversation. I believe at the top of the page there's the end of the conversation from the page before.
