utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- can you tell from the notebook what the date is of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This is after the first conversation but the same date, the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the time of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: 35 minutes past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also indicate what the channel and frequency information for this conversation is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This was on frequency 872.500, channel 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If the usher could show the witness what is marked as P228. And if we can look at the handwritten page which should be /B, I believe, on the ELMO, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you can verify for me that the text that's appearing on the ELMO is a copy of page 0871?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. It's a copy of 0879 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, if we could look at /D of the same exhibit. It should be ... And again, I would ask you if -- in fact, this is the same document you were shown with the last exhibit. And if I can just ask you if it reflects a typed version of the intercept that you have been looking at on that page. This would be the last conversation that appears on this exhibit -- I'm sorry, the second to last.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Well, I don't see the conversation. What I see is the one after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the first page, if I could direct your attention --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: All right. Now I can see it. Yes, it's the same. It's this conversation transcribed on to a computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it appear to be a conversation transcribed on to a computer at your location at Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just one final exercise. You recall meeting with me in our offices on Monday of this week, and I showed you a number of notebooks that you had an opportunity to flip through at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I remember that. I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that I asked you to look through the notebook and see if you could identify your handwriting in them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I also asked you to place a green sticker on the pages where you could identify your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm going to show you those notebooks now one at a time. And if you could just flip to the green sticker on each notebook and let me know if, in fact, the notebook contains your handwriting. We can begin with -- this is Exhibit P340.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see any date in the notebook that would help you identify the time period the notebook is for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning of the notebook, the date is the 13th of June, 1995. I was at Konjuh then and there's another date later on, the 19th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a notebook from Konjuh --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Throughout that period -- this is a notebook from Konjuh and that's where I spent this particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The next is Exhibit P338. If I could ask you to look at that notebook and let me know if you can identify it as a notebook from Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, same thing. During that period of time, I was at Konjuh. Also, there's my friend's handwriting, the one who was with me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The next notebook is P325. And I'm just going to ask you to do the same thing with each one of these notebooks and we'll try to be as quick as we can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. Again, you have a date here. I inserted the date. This is also from Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. This is Exhibit P342.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. This is also from Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. P329.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes. This notebook, too, is from Konjuh. It also bears a date that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry, but because these are notebooks from Konjuh really has no significance to us without some kind of identifying procedure at the first that this notebook represents notations from one period to another period. Otherwise these have absolutely no relevance to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, we may take an example for one of the notebooks. But from the testimony of this witness, I believe that he told us clearly the notebook is recorded at that period of time. But if you want to make more relevant to this case, we may take an example of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I'm happy to have him go through each notebook. I was trying to save some time for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe just one.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's do it with this last one or second to last one is P327.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can tell us, Witness, whether you can identify your handwriting in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you identify the dates for this notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The participants, more specifically -- no, no. I didn't write down a date but my colleagues did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm actually speaking about the notebook itself. If you can tell us what the first date that you can identify in the notebook from the first page on, what the first date is that you can find.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The first one is when the notebook was filed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The date is the 14th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And turning to the back of the notebook, if you can look through the pages there and see if you can identify any date at the back or towards the back.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: On the very next page there is a date, the 3rd of July, 1995. And at the end of the notebook, there is no date but there are frequencies that were taken down during the search of the range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the intercepts that appear in the notebook towards the back of the notebook, is there anything dated that might indicate to you what the end range of the period that this notebook was in use was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This notebook was used from the 3rd of July, 1995. The last date I found is the 23rd of July, 1995, meaning from the 3rd of July to the 23rd of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you mentioned the date, the registration date of the 14th of June earlier. Just for clarification, can you explain what the registration date is of the notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I wasn't the one who did that. There was another man in the company who was in charge of that. This person would register the notebook, give it a number and a date when the handbook was given out, the notebook was given out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the registration date not necessarily coincide with the first date that the notebook was used to transcribe intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: No. The registration date, that was done by a person back at the command. When there was a rotation of the shift, he would send blank notebooks, new notebooks, for us to use out in the field whenever necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do have some cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just have a few questions and they're sort of specific. As I understand it, once the intercepts were written out, the messages were written out, they were then typed out, encrypted, and sent off. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would take it that whoever was doing the typing was supposed to be faithful to what was written down; in other words, they could not or should not take any liberties in typing something that was not or had not been written out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This person could add dots, question marks, just in order to clarify whether the sound was clear or the reason, for example, if a participant could not be heard very clearly. I did not take the whole thing down myself, but the person typing would put dots, and I knew that the other participant could not be heard clearly. So he would just put his own there, you know, he did it. He would write it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just to make sure that I'm clear. The person typing would have the handwritten notebook or notes and he would be typing out, but were they also listening in to what you had picked up, what you had recorded as well, to double check what was written out was consistent with what had been recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Well, no. He didn't check. He just took my notebook and he would transfer it on to a computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if I understand you correctly, there might be some times when they would add a period or some dots, use some punctuation, to make sure that the text was clear. Is that my -- is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: He would type it in the workroom usually. He was there, so he was in a position to ask me whether he should ask me or something else, if there is a question mark at the end of a sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And was punctuation sort of critical or was it getting -- writing down the message the most important aspect of it when you were listening in and trying then to write out what had been recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. As I understand the procedure, and I'll try not to confuse you. But as I understand it, you would record a conversation, and then at some point you would need to write out what had been recorded, what had been tape recorded. My question is: When you would write out, the handwritten portion that was put into the notebooks, in doing that, given the time limitations and the work load, was punctuation a major portion of the transcription or was it something that was just done on an arbitrary basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Well, the most important thing was what was being said, because if you looked at that you could tell if it was a question or -- what do you call that? I always listened to the conversations again and again. If there was a recording of the conversation, I would listen to it again before I started taking it down in the notebook. Then I would rewind to the beginning and I take down all the participants. If I failed to get their names the first time around, then I would take the whole thing down and I would write the conversation that they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you were shown by the Prosecutor what has been marked as P327, that's one of the notebooks. Perhaps it can be provided to you if it's not with you at the moment. Now, if you could be so kind as to turn to the page that is numbered on the left side of the notebook as 00804535, if you could just look at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 4535, that's correct, sir. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, by any chance, is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless you recognise this notebook as being one of the notebooks that was used by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would like to now show you, even though this wasn't yours, but nonetheless the Prosecutor is using you to get this entire notebook into evidence, I would like to now show you what has been marked by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would like to complete the sentence before I get the objection so at least I have my record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What has been marked for identification purposes as P245 and I should note for the record that there is an A, B, C, and D. And we were provided with E, F, G, and H this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has already noted that this was not an intercept that he took down, and I'm not sure it's appropriate to ask him specific questions about intercepts that he did not take down, even if it was from his unit. I will also represent that the intercept operator who did take this intercept down will be appearing before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With that representation, Your Honour, I have no further questions, assuming that they will be bringing that person in so I can confront them with what was written down versus what was sent out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: We would be happy to tell Mr. Karnavas during the next break which witness that is. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a few questions, but if you like I can move to that -- I need the podium to see -- thank you very much. Cross-examined by Ms. Sinatra:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dobar dan, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you -- the counsel for Blagojevic has just said that there are several things that are arbitrary, but the decision as to what conversation is important enough to record and transcribe is totally up to the intercept operator, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I think the witness did not testified to that. And I am not sure that counsel has even accurately represented what Mr. Karnavas said, so I would object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But I remember that Mr. Karnavas asked the same question more or less on this line. Maybe Ms. Sinatra could rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I shall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, but the decision as to what is considered an important enough intercept to record and transcribe is totally a decision made by the intercept operator, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Not in that sense. It's not exclusively his responsibility. We were told to transcribe even a name if it cropped up. So even if it was a name, we would write it down, a new officer, a new secret name of a participant, even though there was no important content to the conversation, even if the conversation was of a private nature, then we wouldn't record it. But the rest we would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your basic direction for monitoring was important people or people who had a lot of command responsibility were considered to be important conversations to intercept. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The people who were important, the officers, their names, if they appeared, then secret names which would come up as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- okay. I'm going to go forward with this. Secret names are the code names you determined for individual people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: The secret names were not used for people. They were used for units which were -- which they had. I'm saying officers if the conversation is not important. If the conversation is not important, if it's of a private nature, they did not have to be transcribed to paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a term that I know you're familiar with. Are you familiar with Operativno Maskiranje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Operativno Maskiranje, I am familiar with masking, but operative masking, I've never encountered that term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And masking is part of your signals unit just daily consideration. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, masking involves misinformation. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: It is deception. That's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's very common in all military structures, especially during combat operations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I don't know how common that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the JNA. It was common with the JNA, too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: We didn't use deception.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't use any kind of planting fake conversations or planting fake names or providing misinformation for the enemy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I would like some clarification about what time period we're talking about. I think it's a little confusing for the witness. She's asking about his service during the early -- or late 1980s in the JNA and then talking about the enemy. I'm not sure who she's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is that important? I think Ms. Sinatra just asked a general question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I will clarify. Only because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the JNA, you were not involved in signals unit or intelligence, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I was a member of the signals unit, but I wasn't a member of an intelligence unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move forward. But you know that with your experience as a member of the signals unit that what you record and what you transcribe not only includes information that may be true, it includes information that may not be true also, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Whether they were correct or not correct, we would transcribe them and pass them on. Our duty was to transcribe the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to refer you to a document that the Prosecution has put in front of you. It was P226. I'm not going to take the Court's time. I'm going to refresh your memory that it was a conversation which I believe you recorded in your own handwriting at 9.05 on the 14th of July. Do you remember seeing that document a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I did see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified earlier about the fact that dot, dot, dot, dots means you couldn't hear the conversation. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: It depends where the dots were. If they were at the beginning of the conversation, it would mean that we didn't catch the beginning. If some word was inaudible or we couldn't hear very well, then we would put the dots there. For example, if one participant was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if the dots are in the middle of a conversation, it means that you couldn't hear that conversation at that time. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Whether we couldn't hear it or perhaps I didn't understand the word, perhaps that could mean that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, too: Generally, if you record a generic statement from, say, Zivanovic, dot, dot, dot, dot, from the duty officer, that duty officer could refer to any of 200 different duty officers on duty on July 14th, 1995, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: Duty officer, I wouldn't know where he was from. I am not thinking or considering who the duty officer was. He's just the duty officer. If I would have known who he was, I would have written it down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also want to know about your shift changes. You said you worked anywhere from seven- to 14-day shifts. Do you remember from refreshing your memory with your log what day your shift change was at your location in July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: My log? I didn't have any log.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what day you changed shifts and got to go home from your location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I can't remember that. There was a logbook before, but I didn't have a logbook for that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't maintain a maintenance record on the equipment either, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: How do you mean, a maintenance record on the equipment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it had been serviced, when it had been repaired.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: No, we didn't conduct these repairs. If some equipment should break down, we would send it out to be repaired or if it was possible to perhaps fix it right there. If it was not possible to fix it right there, we would send it out. There was a workshop for that or sometimes a service person would come by.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go to private session for a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I really appreciate -- we all appreciate the fact that you come here to the Tribunal to testify. The truth is that you do not recognise the voice of Dragan Jokic, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-124
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether I knew him or not. I don't think that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: We have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect, Ms. Davis?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage are there any documents to tender into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's just one document, and that's P351, which is the pseudonym sheet, and that would be tendered under seal. The intercept evidence that was discussed with this witness will be the subject of a later motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, this piece of document is admitted into the evidence. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. I think we have been assisted by your testimony. And I apologise to keep you here for so long and we wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may leave now. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is there someone from the Prosecution team who will brief us about the next witness? Yes? I mean, are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness has demanded to have voice distortion, face distortion, and also pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. Since we need some technical setup, so could we break now and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have some problem with the microphone. Would you please say something to the microphone, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Viada.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Defence counsels. Examined by Mr. Viada:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. First of all, I would like to request the usher's assistance in order to provide you a particular exhibit in which you can find your name written on it. I would like you to say if your name is, in fact, written on this paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I see something that is very much like my name on this piece of paper, however, it does contain certain errors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there is another name on that paper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Shall we go to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Judges something about your educational background briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I completed a secondary school for engineers, a technical school, and a high school for engineers. I am a technician. I am an engineer. That's my education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of engineer are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I'm a mining engineer and a mechanical engineer, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to move quickly to the time of your -- the time that you serviced in the army, the time of the war. When did you join the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I joined the army in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What unit of the Bosnian army did you join at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: It was the 3rd Brigade of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in that unit since 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I stayed with that unit until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened in August 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: In August 1994, I received an order from the commander to be transferred to a different unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: That was the electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you given training prior to your operational service in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: From mid-September that year to mid-October that year, there was a one-month course, training. We were trained to operate the equipment used by this unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us which kind of training did you receive, very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: This training was basically an introduction to radio technology. We were being trained to use the equipment. There were several subjects being discussed that were indispensable for an operator. We needed to know how to operate the equipment without damaging the equipment, and we who attended the course were not specially trained people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any experience in radio communications before that training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain with the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I remained in the army from December 1992 to April 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the help of Madam Usher, I would like to show the witness Exhibit 318, please. Could you point on that exhibit the location of the unit in which you were working from August 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: The unit was at Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To who was your unit -- to whom was your unit directly subordinated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: It was a unit of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you tell the Judges very briefly, because the Judges have heard from a number of witnesses on the same point, what was the purpose of that unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Basically, the unit had two objectives. The only objective of the unit was to protect the population and the military. This was done by electronic surveillance, which in this case came down to listening in on conversations being transmitted on enemy frequencies and interfering with the enemy's communications which was less often the case. Usually there were combat operations underway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in your unit in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I don't know how many people there were. I don't know how many people were in the company, in the company for the -- for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare, but I can tell you how many people there were in my own group. The number varied from 5 to 15, depending on the situation we were facing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you organise the work in your platoon, in your unit, at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: My detachment was one of two of our platoon, the platoon that was based at Okresanica. We had two detachments there. And those two took turns in carrying out these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking to go into private session for a couple of minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with codes for coded language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I must say I don't quite understand your question. Can you please elucidate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Are you familiar with coded languages, I mean deciphering codes or coded languaging, communications, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: If what you mean is code names denoting certain units of the enemy, in that case, yes, I am familiar with those code names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. From the question I just would like, for clarification purposes, coding is not the same as encryption, which is another form of coding with the military. If we could just delineate that with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we have already come across this issue many times. You may proceed, Mr. Viada.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please, can you tell the Judges how did you become familiar with this code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I became familiar with the codes, as all soldiers who monitored those conversations. This was done on the basis of experience during our monitoring of the conversations. We memorised certain participants in certain locations as well as certain units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell Their Honours very shortly about the details of the procedure that you followed when you were working in that unit in Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Our unit monitored radio relay communications of the enemy. These were used to transmit telephone conversations. We had in our possession amateur equipment specially adapted or modified to catch those conversations. So we continually monitored the activity on those channels. Whenever there was a conversation that we caught and believed was relevant, we recorded the conversation on a reel-to-reel recorder. The next step would be to transcribe or write down the contents of the conversation from the reel-to-reel recorder into a notebook. This notebook contained the information that we had recorded on tape. The notebook would then be passed on to the encryption section, the encryption unit, who were, in their turn, in touch with the corps command. There was a soldier in that unit who typed up the text or the message on to a computer and sent it on to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just only a couple of things about this procedure. How did you decide which was an important or a relevant conversation that you have heard in order to be recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: The relevance of a conversation could be determined in a number of different ways. The equipment we used for the tapping had certain fixed channels related to certain strategic positions, localities, of the enemy. It was very important for us what was happening on those channels, those specific channels. If, for example, we had four conversations going at the same time, we were paying special attention to what was happening on the first three channels, because that's where the enemy was sharing information. But also, the other channels were important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you write down the conversations that you were intercepting verbatim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Any conversation occurring on such channels -- any conversation by people whose voices we could identify or if there was anything else for us to indicate that it was an important conversation, we would automatically decide to record the conversation. We had no time to write it down. The fundamental thing for us was to record it and then perhaps to transcribe it and eventually send it on to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in the process of transcribing the conversations that you first had intercepted, did you transcribe these conversations usually word-by-word?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: The command ordered us clearly to insist on the accuracy of the information that we were passing on. The established practice was that the soldier who first caught the conversation then copied the conversation literally into a notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then would you hear a conversation more than one time, if necessary, before writing it down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: We faced a number of different situations, depending on the quality of reception, depending on the pronunciation of the participants involved. Sometimes it was possible to transcribe a conversation after listening to it once or twice, but sometimes this took hours and we needed help from our colleagues in order to be able to understand clearly what the participants were saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was part of your duties to check the conversation typed down by the soldier, so as to verify the accuracy of the transcription?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: The army evolved. There were two different kinds of approach depending on the exact period of this evolution. At one point in time, they asked to run checks and to verify information. However, we were often short of men and sort of time to do all these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you wouldn't do this frequently or sometimes or never? Which is your answer of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Generally speaking, all the soldiers were trusted and everyone was responsible for their work. Sometimes verification would only mean checking the orthography, so in answer to your question I can say that I didn't do this very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Was it part of your job to analyse the conversations that you were listening to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: In principle, our job would be finished as soon as we forwarded a conversation to the soldier who was in charge of typing it up on to a computer and sending it on to the command. Then there were other people with the command who analysed the conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to make the last question about the procedure. What would you do with the tapes used? Did you re-use the tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: At one point in time, we passed the tapes on to the command. This usually took a while. However, as time went by sometimes there were tapes that we ended up not forwarding. To all practical intents, the reason was that there weren't enough tapes. So we had to use the same tapes twice to record the conversation and to then transcribe the conversation into the notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we can right now go to another subject, which is the notebooks that you wrote down while you were working in that unit. First of all, I would like the witness to be shown the notebook the Exhibit 322, please, with the help of Madam Usher. In the page numbered 00778845, can you recognise that page your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Yes, there is a text on this page that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a conversation that was intercepted by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which are the time in which that conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Each conversation that was recorded in the notebook had to have the time when the conversation took place and the channel and the frequency where the conversation was intercepted. So this particular conversation was intercepted at 1658 hours. So it began at 1658 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same notebook, which the name 00778906, do you recognise your handwriting in that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: There is a part of the text on this page which was written by my hand. It's a text that began at 0834 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this text continues in the next pages or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: On the next page is another conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then when you say this page 906 -- ending 906, the number, you see part of a conversation, a whole conversation, or it is the beginning or the end of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: On this page with the conversation of 0834 hours, it's an entire conversation. It was supposed to be a contact that was supposed to be established between two friendly units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If the witness could be shown another exhibit, in particular the Exhibit 345. The page 01077809, can you recognise your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Yes. The text on this page is a text that I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time do you see in that conversation, the conversation to have taken place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: This conversation started at 2227 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to go --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to go to the second page of the notebook, which is evidence unit number 1 -- 0107770. Can you see a date in that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Yes, I do see a date on this page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does this date mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: This date means that starting from this day, the book was made available for the recording, the writing, of these reports or the materials that were transcribed from the tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date that you see on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: On this page, the date is the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today in my office, you have had the opportunity to go through this particular notebook. I'm going to ask you: According with the procedure that you used to fill the notebook, can you determine the date of the particular conversation that you intercepted at 2227 hours? I mean the one that you recognised before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: The day when the message -- the conversation was intercepted can be determined in principle starting from this date and from the time when the first conversation was transcribed. All the conversations have the time when they were intercepted, when they began, and this time gives the possibility for the reports to be separated into the days on which they were made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so, can you be precise and tell the Judges when that particular conversation that you were shown before was intercepted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: In order to tell you this information, I have to look at all the conversations according to their times, and based on that we can note -- so if we have the first conversation in this notebook was registered at 2115 hours, it means that on that day we began to use the book and the first date in that case is the 12th of July. The next day, the 13th of July, the first recorded conversation was taken in 0805 hours, this is for the 13th of July -- the 13th of July ends with a conversation at 2153 hours. The next conversation for the 14th of July began at 0704 hours. So the conversation at 2227 hours took place on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I'm going to direct your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 233/F. And the translation which is 233/A, I believe. 233/F. I would request not to put this on the record, because it has the name of the witness on it. Is that document, the conversation -- is this document familiar to you? Have you seen this document or this kind of document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: This document is a document that was transferred into the computer. It was copied from the notebook that I was looking at just a little while earlier. The time, 2227 hours, channel 3. So this is a conversation from that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this format? I mean, you have seen these kinds of documents -- with the indepedence of this particular document, are you familiar with the format of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I had the rare opportunity to see some documents which had been typed into our computer at Okresanica, and I believe that this is a document from that computer, since the document also contains numbers below the text which I gave and said that they should be entered below the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you can right now be shown Exhibit 231/E. Can you see the date in the top of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Yes, I see a date at the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: It's the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown again the former exhibit at the same time with this document, please. In all these documents, I mean Exhibit 231/E and Exhibit 233/F, do you think there is a kind of continuance? I mean, is the same document with several pages according to the things that you are having the opportunity to read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: If you mean to compare the two documents which I have on the desk, so the document which was recorded on channel 5 with a heading of the military and the document recorded from channel 3 with no heading at all, I believe that these two documents are two different documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you think are both documents part of the same bunch of documents or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt the flow, but I will object. I believe the gentleman indicated they are from two different sources. Now, if he wishes to say whether he believes it's part of the same conversation, and maybe that's what the gentleman wished to get out, the Prosecutor, that is. That may be an appropriate question, but I think the witness indicated that they're from two different sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Viada, I think you could ask some questions along the line the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to withdraw this question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to the text of this particular intercept, in this particular intercept, you -- I mean the intercept which starts out 2227 hours you wrote down "Jokic duty officer from Palma." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm going to have to object to the leading form of the question,. He can ask him what he wrote down but he can't put the words in the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think everybody has that document in front of us. I think your client's name was there, so I don't think there's a big problem for that. But, Mr. Viada, you could ask the witness who wrote down this name and how did he know it is that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what Palma was code of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Palma was the code name for the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Right now if the witness could be shown again Exhibit 345, which is the notebook. Can you see at page 01077809, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: I see the same conversation as before of 2227.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If the witness could be shown right now another notebook, notebook 91, please, Exhibit 333. Can you look at the page which ends in 0633, please. Do you recognise your handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We got the answer, but if the gentleman could be cautioned if he recognises the handwriting as opposed does he recognise his handwriting. It's a slight technicality, but I think it might get more complicated as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's a right point. And, Mr. Viada, you may ask whose handwriting is this? And then it depends on the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same notebook, can we turn to page 00800632, please. Whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: This page also contains my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the same notebook, please, the number of the page ending 652. Can you tell the Judges whose handwriting is this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: This is also my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we can turn, with the help of the usher, to the last notebook, which is Exhibit 330. Can the witness be shown page 753, please. Whose handwriting is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Viada, you showed a notebook, but you have to tell us where is the corresponding transcripts, you know, for this intercept, otherwise we'll get lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Okay. If -- can I help to read for the record all the transcripts which pertains to these particular notebooks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you may tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. Just for the record only to mention that notebook 1 is the Exhibit 171/C. Notebook -- Exhibit 345 is Exhibit 233/D, which is notebook 232. Again, notebook 232, Exhibit 255/F. Notebook -- no, Exhibit 235/4 which is notebook 232 is Exhibit 255/F --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There is no notebook 232, and I want to make sure Exhibit P232 doesn't get confused with what he says is notebook 232. It's line 32 in the transcript, and it's confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could provide a complete note could be some kind of help to the Court with all the dates of the reference of these particular notebooks and pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that, you know, in the transcript we have to understand which is corresponding to which one, you know, so that we could have a complete record so everybody will know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: You are right, Your Honour. Let me check them more carefully. May I ask for 2 minutes in order to be more accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Notebook -- Exhibit 171, corresponding Exhibit 322. Exhibit 233, corresponding Exhibit 345. Exhibit 237, corresponding Exhibit 322. Exhibit 255, corresponding Exhibit 345. Exhibit 257, corresponding Exhibit 333. Exhibit 258, corresponding Exhibit 333. Exhibit 285, corresponding Exhibit 91. Exhibit 289, corresponding Exhibit 339. Exhibit 291, corresponding Exhibit 345. And Exhibit 309 is corresponding with Exhibit 330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hope everybody gets it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But, Mr. Viada, to facilitate the work, what if you submit a list tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I may need a moment, given the last moment we had. Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good evening, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Good evening to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just have a few questions and as I understand it you came by this position, the one that we've been discussing, I take it as a result of your education; in other words, that they selected you back in 1994 and they trained you to be in this particular position as an intercept operator. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were fairly well educated and though you didn't any particular background in radio communications, they nonetheless felt that because of your level of education that you would adopt to this position. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: This was an assessment of the command, not my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Viada.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but if we can go into private session it would be a good idea at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you need that, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think I understand the gentleman's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe we just furnished Madam Usher with those -- with copies of D75/1 and D76/1. And while the papers are being distributed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just look at the handwritten version that is found in what is marked as P255/E and look at the typewritten version in what is marked as P255/D, and please tell me if they correspond.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: If I understand this, you want me to compare the handwritten text in the upper left corner of the page to the text in capital letters written out as a report to the right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I want to make sure that you can compare the two, look at them, compare them, to see whether we're talking about the same intercept, one being handwritten, the other one having been typed out, which I assume was encrypted and then sent off later on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that the handwritten conversation encircled in the upper left portion of the page is part of a conversation that was typed up on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, to make sure that you're looking at the right part, if you flip -- if you would in the handwritten version, if you would turn to the second page and look at the top left-hand corner, and I believe it's -- it has 01077831. And you will see that it is marked out, highlighted, blocked out, call it whatever you wish, it's on the left side of that notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: So you mean the document -- oh, right. I don't understand this. Can you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. This -- the page that I'm asking you to look at which is marked for identification purposes as 255/1F, which apparently is from the notebook 345, your notebook, the one that you identified, on that particular page there seems to be a blocked out portion which describes the channel, the hours as 1847, and the individuals that seem to be having a discussion. I then asked you to look at a typewritten version which is marked as P255/D in the middle of the page, and it would seem that perhaps the -- it is a typewritten version of the handwritten version. And I'm asking you to look at them and to tell me whether I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. These two texts that were marked off, one handwritten and the other typed up on a computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if you look at the handwritten version, one would assume, given the procedure or the practice that was in place, the handwritten version would have come first and then the typewritten version. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Well, again I must say these two conversations that are marked out, the first one is a handwritten version and the other one is typed up on channel 5 where the exact time given here. These are two different conversations, if that's what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting that -- are you suggesting that the typewritten version comes from some place other than the handwritten version? In other words, that some other unit did the same thing, or is the typewritten version generated as a result of the handwritten version, which is found in the notebook which you've identified as being a notebook that was generated and completed while you were the commander of that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: In answer to your question, I can only say what I know for certain. I know that I was the one who wrote this text. As for what happened later and who did what with this text, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the text that you wrote, is that a verbatim conversation that you monitored as the procedure or the practice that was set out pursuant to the orders that you had received, or does it appear to be a summary of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: When we talk about the presentation of intercepts, at stage 1 we have information concerning the time and place as well as the participants. Those are three different times. We have two comments. If we stick blindly to the logic that we should transcribe everything we hear, we should have several million people on the job. If, on the other hand, there is anything that would indicate any information of relevance without containing anything else, then this would be within our remit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me, would you not, that what I am showing you right now is quite contrary to what you represented earlier, both on direct and on cross-examination, when you said that you would -- you and your colleagues would faithfully write down verbatim what was heard, because those were the orders, the orders which you had indicated were to follow and I take it you were instructing your subordinates to follow. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120
utterances.text: Well, in order to give an order and to make it executive, the side observing a problem, considering a problem, must be familiar with the technical possibilities and the area in which the information occurs. If you say that a million citizens are being tapped, that their phones are being tapped, on a daily basis, then the reverse of that is how many citizens does it take to tap into the conversations of a million different citizens. If you give an order to someone to take down whatever they heard in a given conversation, every single thing they heard, then certainly the least that would be required for that is several million people on the job just for the transcription itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we have 10 minutes past the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, and I'm afraid, Your Honour, in light of -- I had hopped to do a quite short cross-examination, but I'm afraid I'm not going to be able to finish as quickly. I thought it was only going to be a 5-minute or a 10-minute cross, but now I'm compelled to do a rather more aggressive cross-examination in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, save it for tomorrow afternoon. Well, Witness, as I did with all the other witnesses, I have to tell you that you are under the oath, so do not tell anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I'm very grateful to the interpreters and the technicians behind this courtroom for their indulgence to let us stay in this courtroom for 10 minutes more. And we'll resume tomorrow afternoon. The hearing is adjourned.
